header.contentArea: Applied surgical science and critical care
guidelineVersions: UKKA Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults (July 2020; updated Oct 2023 and July 2026)

related.why: Fluids, electrolytes and AKI after abdominal surgery

brief.scenario: Mr Dennis Hale, 71, is on day 3 after a laparotomy and Hartmann's procedure. His ramipril was restarted yesterday. He has passed 90 ml of urine in the last 6 hours. The lab phones: potassium 7.1 mmol/L (not haemolysed), creatinine 246 µmol/L (baseline 92).
brief.task: The examiner will ask how you would manage him, and will read out his ECG findings.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Severe hyperkalaemia with AKI: protect the heart, shift potassium, remove it, monitor, and fix the cause.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Giving insulin without calcium when the ECG is abnormal, or forgetting the glucose afterwards.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd see him now, attach a monitor and get a 12-lead ECG."

grid.label: Initial assessment and monitoring
grid.fail: Treats by phone without seeing him or getting an ECG.
grid.pass: Sees him now: ABCDE, NEWS2, 12-lead ECG, continuous cardiac monitoring; blood gas for a rapid potassium; recognises 6.5 or more as severe.
grid.high: Moves him to a monitored bed, and treats on the gas result rather than waiting for a repeat lab sample.

grid.label: ECG interpretation
grid.fail: Calls the ECG findings normal or can't name any hyperkalaemic change.
grid.pass: Interprets the written findings as peaked T waves, flattened P waves, prolonged PR and a broad QRS.
grid.high: Knows the sequence can jump straight to a sine wave, bradycardia or arrest; the ECG doesn't track the level reliably.

grid.label: IV calcium first (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Omits calcium despite ECG changes, or gives it only after the insulin.
grid.pass: IV calcium first: 30 ml 10% calcium gluconate over 10 minutes (or 10 ml 10% calcium chloride over 5 minutes).
grid.high: Knows calcium doesn't lower potassium, works within 3 minutes, lasts 30–60 minutes; repeats the ECG and considers a further dose.

grid.label: Shifting potassium
grid.fail: Gives salbutamol alone, or gets the insulin dose wrong.
grid.pass: 10 units soluble insulin in 25 g glucose (50 ml of 50%) IV over 5–15 minutes; nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg as an adjunct.
grid.high: Checks pre-treatment glucose: below 7.0, adds 10% glucose at 50 ml/h for 5 hours; starts sodium zirconium cyclosilicate.

grid.label: Glucose monitoring (safety-critical)
grid.pass: Monitors capillary glucose regularly for 6 hours after insulin-glucose.
grid.high: States the schedule: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 minutes, then hourly to 6 hours; treats hypoglycaemia below 4.0 mmol/L.

grid.label: Repeat potassium and culprit drugs
grid.fail: Doesn't recheck potassium, or leaves the ramipril prescribed.
grid.pass: Repeats potassium at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 hours; stops ramipril and any potassium supplements or added KCl.
grid.high: Checks for NSAIDs and potassium-sparing diuretics, and watches for rebound as the insulin wears off.

grid.label: Treating the AKI and escalating
grid.fail: Corrects the potassium but ignores the AKI.
grid.pass: Assesses volume, fluid challenge if dry, catheter and fluid balance; stops nephrotoxins; tells the registrar and renal or critical care team.
grid.high: Refers immediately for renal replacement therapy if potassium doesn't respond; ultrasound within 24 hours if obstruction possible; looks for sepsis.

fail.text: How would you manage Mr Hale?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd ask the nurse to give him some insulin and dextrose and I'll recheck the potassium in the morning.

fail.speaker: examiner

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you manage Mr Hale?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This is severe hyperkalaemia, 6.5 or more. I'd see him now: ABCDE, NEWS2, a 12-lead ECG, cardiac monitoring, and a blood gas for a quick potassium.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: I'll read out his ECG findings.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Those are peaked T waves, flattened P waves, a long PR and a broad QRS.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: IV calcium to protect the heart: 30 ml of 10% calcium gluconate over 10 minutes.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Then 10 units of soluble insulin in 25 g of glucose over 5 to 15 minutes, and nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg as an adjunct.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd monitor his glucose regularly for 6 hours afterwards.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Repeat potassium at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 hours. Stop the ramipril and any potassium supplements or added KCl.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: For the AKI: assess his fluid status, fluid challenge if dry, catheter and fluid balance, stop nephrotoxins. I'd tell my registrar and the renal team.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would you manage Mr Hale?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Potassium 7.1 is severe, and with an AKI it may still be rising. I'd see him now, ABCDE and NEWS2, get him on a monitor in a monitored bed, a 12-lead ECG, and a gas so I'm not waiting for the lab.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: I'll read out his ECG findings.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Tall peaked T waves, flat P waves, a long PR, and the QRS is broadening. That's dangerous: it can go straight to a sine wave or bradycardic arrest.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: 30 ml of 10% calcium gluconate over 10 minutes. It stabilises the myocardium within minutes but doesn't lower potassium and lasts 30 to 60 minutes, so I'd repeat the ECG and give more if the changes persist.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Then 10 units of Actrapid in 50 ml of 50% glucose over 5 to 15 minutes. His glucose was 5.8, below 7, so I'd follow it with 10% glucose at 50 ml an hour for 5 hours. Salbutamol 10 to 20 mg nebulised as an adjunct, and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate to remove potassium.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Capillary glucose at 0, 30, 60, 90 and 120 minutes, then hourly to 6 hours. Below 4 I'd treat it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Potassium at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 hours, watching for rebound. Stop the ramipril, any added potassium, and any NSAIDs or spironolactone.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The AKI is the driver: volume assessment, fluid challenge if he's dry, catheter, look for sepsis or a leak. Registrar and renal or critical care now; if potassium doesn't respond, he needs renal replacement therapy.

failures.move: Giving insulin-glucose without IV calcium when the ECG shows hyperkalaemic changes.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: the myocardium is unprotected while potassium falls slowly; he can arrest.
Safety-critical: hypoglycaemia is the frequent harm of this treatment and can go unrecognised.

failures.move: Normalising the potassium without treating the AKI.
failures.consequence: Potassium rebounds and he may need renal replacement therapy late.

recovery.line: Before the insulin, I'd give IV calcium because the ECG is abnormal.
I'd check the trust hyperkalaemia protocol and give calcium first while I do.

knowledge.fact: Severe hyperkalaemia is 6.5 mmol/L or more; moderate 6.0–6.4.
ECG changes: 30 ml 10% calcium gluconate over 10 minutes, or 10 ml 10% calcium chloride over 5 minutes in resuscitation.
10 units soluble insulin in 25 g glucose; if pre-treatment glucose is below 7.0, 10% glucose at 50 ml/h for 5 hours. Monitor glucose for 6 hours.
Refer immediately for renal replacement therapy if hyperkalaemia isn't responding to medical management.

recall.think: Arrest from hyperkalaemia; hypoglycaemia from its treatment.
recall.say: "ECG changes: IV calcium now, then insulin-glucose."
do: Glucose for 6 hours; repeat K; stop ramipril
recall.finish: Treat the AKI; renal replacement therapy if refractory.

sources.name: UK Kidney Association Clinical Practice Guidelines: Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults (Alfonzo A, Harrison A, Baines R, et al.)
sources.version: Original July 2020; updated October 2023 and July 2026 (review October 2026)
sources.supports: Mild 5.5-5.9, moderate 6.0-6.4, severe 6.5 mmol/l or more; 12-lead ECG if K 6.0 or more (14.1); continuous monitoring if 6.5 or more or ECG changes (14.2); point-of-care blood gas K (15.2); IV calcium with ECG changes: 30 ml 10% calcium gluconate over 10 minutes or 10 ml 10% calcium chloride over 5 minutes (16.2a), chloride in resuscitation, gluconate otherwise (16.2b); effect within 3 minutes, lasts 30-60 minutes; insulin-glucose 10 units soluble insulin in 25 g glucose (16.3.1), given over 5-15 minutes (appendix 4B); if pre-treatment glucose below 7.0 mmol/l, 10% glucose 50 ml/h for 5 hours (16.3.3); nebulised salbutamol 10-20 mg as adjunct, not monotherapy (16.4.1-16.4.3); sodium zirconium cyclosilicate for severe hyperkalaemia (16.6.1a); K at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 h (17.1.2); glucose at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, 300 and 360 minutes (17.2); hypoglycaemia defined as below 4.0 mmol/l; withhold RAAS inhibitors in acute illness (2.6); stop drugs that potentiate hyperkalaemia, e.g. potassium supplements, NSAIDs, potassium-sparing diuretics (Table 32); renal or critical care referral if severe (19.1). July 2026 update: IV calcium evidence grade lowered to 2C after ILCOR 2025; doses and rates unchanged

sources.name: NICE NG148: Acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management
sources.supports: Consider stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in vomiting or sepsis (1.2.14); urgent ultrasound within 24 hours if no cause or risk of obstruction (1.4.6); discuss renal replacement therapy immediately with a nephrologist or critical care (1.5.6); refer immediately for RRT if hyperkalaemia, acidosis, uraemic complications, fluid overload or pulmonary oedema are not responding to medical management (1.5.8)

partner.opening: Mr Hale's potassium has just been phoned through. How would you manage him?

reveals.finding: NEWS2 4: pulse 58, BP 96/60, RR 22, SpO2 96% on air, temperature 37.6°C, alert.

Read out: the 12-lead ECG shows a regular rhythm at 58 per minute, with a P wave before every QRS complex. The P waves are small and flattened. PR interval 240 ms. QRS duration 130 ms. The T waves across the chest leads are tall, narrow-based, symmetrical and pointed.
K 7.0, pH 7.29, bicarbonate 17, lactate 2.1, glucose 5.8 mmol/L.

reveals.trigger: Asks about the drug chart and fluids
reveals.finding: Ramipril 5 mg restarted yesterday; Hartmann's running; regular paracetamol; ibuprofen as needed.
At 1 hour: K 6.2; ECG changes improved; glucose 4.6.

push.question: Why calcium, if it doesn't lower potassium?
push.expect: Stabilises the myocardium within minutes; given first when the ECG is abnormal.

push.question: What is the main hazard of insulin-glucose, and how do you prevent it?
push.expect: Hypoglycaemia: extra 10% glucose if pre-treatment glucose is below 7.0, and glucose checks for 6 hours.

push.question: When would he need dialysis?
push.expect: Hyperkalaemia, acidosis, uraemic complications or fluid overload not responding to medical treatment.

curveballs.prompt: He becomes bradycardic at 34 and loses his output.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Cardiac arrest: call the arrest team, ALS; IV calcium chloride 10 ml 10% and insulin-glucose as a reversible cause.

curveballs.prompt: Would you give Hartmann's? It contains potassium.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Hartmann's contains only 5 mmol/L potassium and isn't the cause. Stop potassium supplements or added KCl; choose fluid by volume status and acid–base (he is acidotic), and follow local guidance.

curveballs.prompt: At 4 hours the potassium is back up to 6.8 despite treatment.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Refractory: repeat treatment, and refer immediately to renal or critical care for renal replacement therapy.
